0.title: The Kinsman-Redeemer: The Book of Ruth
0.overview:
The book of Ruth is a small, bright story set in a very dark age. It opens "in the days when the judges ruled" (1:1), an era Judges sums up as "everyone did what was right in his own eyes." Yet in the same dark soil God is quietly growing a story of loyal love, courageous faith and redemption that ends at the cradle of King David and, beyond him, at the manger of David's greater Son. God is often most at work when his hand seems most hidden.

At the center stands the Hebrew word hesed: covenant loyalty, steadfast love, grace that stays faithful beyond what duty demands. It is the word used of God's own faithfulness, and in Ruth it takes human shape: in Ruth's vow to Naomi, in Boaz's generosity, in the way the whole story turns out.

When was Ruth written? The author is not named (a Jewish tradition suggested Samuel). It was written after David was born (4:22), for readers who needed an old custom explained (4:7); most date it to the time of the kings, some later, and the question is open. It presents itself as history, told with great art, and Matthew names Ruth in the line of Christ (Matt 1:5). The Hebrew Bible places it among the Writings; English Bibles follow the Greek order and put it after Judges.

How could a Moabite enter Israel, when the law barred Moabites from the assembly (Deut 23:3)? Jewish tradition read the law as applying to Moabite men. The deeper answer is that Ruth came as a convert who took Israel’s God as her own (1:16), and faith brought her in, as it brought Rahab. The law excluded Moab for its hostility to God’s people; Ruth renounced it. Her place in David’s line shows that God’s grace reaches the outsider who trusts him.

The theological heart of the book is the go'el, the kinsman-redeemer: a near relative with the right to redeem a destitute family member, to buy back land, to rescue from slavery, to raise up an heir for a dead kinsman. Boaz is a pattern of Christ the Redeemer that a careful reader may gladly see. The New Testament does not name Boaz as a type (an advance picture of Christ), but it calls Christ our Redeemer and makes him our kinsman, sharing our flesh and blood and not ashamed to call us brothers (Heb 2:11–17; Gal 4:4–5). Boaz had the right to redeem (he was a kinsman), the resources (he was wealthy), and the willingness. He did not have to; he chose to, out of love. So the eternal Son had every right, paid the price with his own precious blood, and was willing: he said, "I delight to do your will, O my God" (Ps 40:8). The likeness lies in the redeemer’s role and heart; the threshing floor, the barley and the sandal belong to the story and are not hidden symbols.

And Ruth is a foreigner, drawn under the wings of the God of Israel by sheer grace. The barrier between Jew and Gentile, which the cross would one day demolish (Eph 2:13–14), is already being undermined in a barley field outside Bethlehem. Read it slowly: in it the steadfast love of the LORD shines out of the darkness, and a Redeemer steps forward who will not let his bride remain empty.

1.title: Emptied and Returning
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the days when the judges ruled there was a famine in the land, and a man of Bethlehem in Judah went to sojourn in the country of Moab, he and his wife and his two sons.<sup>2</sup>The name of the man was Elimelech and the name of his wife Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They went into the country of Moab and remained there.<sup>3</sup>But Elimelech, the husband of Naomi, died, and she was left with her two sons.<sup>4</sup>These took Moabite wives; the name of the one was Orpah and the name of the other Ruth. They lived there about ten years,<sup>5</sup>and both Mahlon and Chilion died, so that the woman was left without her two sons and her husband.<sup>6</sup>Then she arose with her daughters-in-law to return from the country of Moab, for she had heard in the fields of Moab that the LORD had visited his people and given them food.<sup>7</sup>So she set out from the place where she was with her two daughters-in-law, and they went on the way to return to the land of Judah.<sup>8</sup>But Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go, return each of you to her mother's house. May the LORD deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me.<sup>9</sup>The LORD grant that you may find rest, each of you in the house of her husband!" Then she kissed them, and they lifted up their voices and wept.<sup>10</sup>And they said to her, "No, we will return with you to your people."<sup>11</sup>But Naomi said, "Turn back, my daughters; why will you go with me? Have I yet sons in my womb that they may become your husbands?<sup>12</sup>Turn back, my daughters; go your way, for I am too old to have a husband. If I should say I have hope, even if I should have a husband this night and should bear sons,<sup>13</sup>would you therefore wait till they were grown? Would you therefore refrain from marrying? No, my daughters, for it is exceedingly bitter to me for your sake that the hand of the LORD has gone out against me."<sup>14</sup>Then they lifted up their voices and wept again. And Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth clung to her.<sup>15</sup>And she said, "See, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and to her gods; return after your sister-in-law."<sup>16</sup>But Ruth said, "Do not urge me to leave you or to return from following you. For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.<sup>17</sup>Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried. May the LORD do so to me and more also if anything but death parts me from you."<sup>18</sup>And when Naomi saw that she was determined to go with her, she said no more.<sup>19</sup>So the two of them went on until they came to Bethlehem. And when they came to Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them. And the women said, "Is this Naomi?"<sup>20</sup>She said to them, "Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.<sup>21</sup>I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi, when the LORD has testified against me and the Almighty has brought calamity upon me?"<sup>22</sup>So Naomi returned, and Ruth the Moabite her daughter-in-law with her, who returned from the country of Moab. And they came to Bethlehem at the beginning of barley harvest.
1.overview:
Chapter 1 is a chapter of emptying. It opens with famine in Bethlehem, "the house of bread" with no bread, and a family that flees to Moab to survive. There Elimelech dies, then both sons, and Naomi is stripped of husband, children and future. She will name the contrast herself: "I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty" (1:21). Here is grief told without flinching, the bitterness of a believer wounded by God's providence who does not pretend otherwise.

Against this darkness shines one of the most luminous commitments in the Old Testament. At the crossroads, where Orpah turns back, reasonably and understandably, Ruth clings to Naomi: "your people shall be my people, and your God my God." This is not passing feeling but a binding promise, sealed with an oath. A Moabite woman with no earthly reason for hope throws in her lot with the God of Israel. This is conversion, grace producing loyalty.

Naomi sees only the LORD's heavy hand, and she is not wrong that he is sovereign over her sorrow. But the narrator closes with a quiet detail, the beginning of barley harvest (1:22), and in those fields God is already preparing to fill her.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Family Emptied in Moab
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Famine drives Elimelech and his family from Bethlehem to Moab. There, over a decade, Elimelech dies, his two sons marry Moabite women, and then both sons die, leaving three childless widows: Naomi, Orpah, and Ruth.
verseByVerse.theology: The opening verses set the book's tension between fullness and emptiness and raise the hard question of how God rules over suffering. The narrator does not explicitly condemn the move to Moab, but three funerals in five verses cast a shadow. Moab was a dangerous place for Israel’s faith (Num 25). Yet God's sovereignty stands over the whole episode; even the deaths that empty Naomi are dark threads from which he will weave redemption.
verseByVerse.examples: Naomi's family did what families have always done in crisis: they sought survival wherever it could be found, even at the cost of leaving the covenant land and people. Ruth offers no cheap answers to why God's people suffer. It shows a family in ruins, and asks the grieving reader only to keep reading.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days when the judges ruled there was a famine in the land, and a man of Bethlehem in Judah went to sojourn in the country of Moab, he and his wife and his two sons. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In the days when the judges ruled" places us in the most spiritually chaotic era of Israel's history, summarized as "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (Judg 21:25). It is in that darkness that God works this jewel of a story.

Then a stinging irony: famine, and the man is from Bethlehem, "house of bread." Famine in the land of promise is often a sign that God is withdrawing his blessing because the nation has broken his covenant (Deut 28). Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, a people descended from Lot's incestuous union (Gen 19) and a long-standing enemy of Israel. Yet God's providence is not confined to Bethlehem; he governs even the wanderings of those who stray, and Moab will become the soil where a flower of faith blooms. The story begins in emptiness, but it begins in the hands of God.

Was the move to Moab a sin? The text does not condemn it outright; Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had all gone abroad in famine. But a short stay became a settled home (v. 2), and the sons married Moabite women. The drift away from the land of promise is the quiet warning.
verseByVerse.note: Ruth is set in the time of the judges, before Israel had a king.

verseByVerse.quote: The name of the man was Elimelech and the name of his wife Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They went into the country of Moab and remained there. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Hebrew the names speak. "Elimelech" means "My God is King," a beautiful confession, yet the man bearing it leaves the land where God reigns. "Naomi" means "pleasant," a name she will renounce in her bitterness (1:20). "Mahlon" and "Chilion" are associated with sickness and wasting away, names that whisper of the deaths to come. The family are Ephrathites, an honored clan of Bethlehem, the Ephrathah of Micah 5:2 from which the Messiah would come.

"Remained there" is quietly damning. A temporary sojourn becomes a settled life in Moab. That is how compromise so often works: not by a single decisive rebellion, but by a gradual settling into a place we were never meant to stay. The narrator offers no comment, only the facts, and God is already preparing a redemption no one can yet see.
verseByVerse.note: Ephrath was an older name for the Bethlehem area (Gen 35:19).

verseByVerse.quote: But Elimelech, the husband of Naomi, died, and she was left with her two sons. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first blow falls. The man whose name proclaimed "My God is King" is gone, and the narrator’s few words deepen the grief.

Now the story is told from Naomi’s side: “she was left”, a survivor being stripped of her family. A widow’s security lay in her husband and then in her sons; Naomi’s survival now hangs on two sons whose names suggest sickness.

Providence, God’s rule over all that happens, does not make God the author of evil, but it does mean that nothing, not even bereavement in a foreign land, falls outside his governance. Naomi cannot yet see it, but the God who is King even when his servant has left the land where he reigns is at work in her loss.

The emptying has begun, and the worst is not yet over. Scripture tells grief honestly; it does not airbrush what God's people really endure.

verseByVerse.quote: These took Moabite wives; the name of the one was Orpah and the name of the other Ruth. They lived there about ten years, and both Mahlon and Chilion died, so that the woman was left without her two sons and her husband. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For about ten years there is the appearance of stability. But these marriages were outside the covenant people, with women from a nation the law barred from Israel’s assembly (Deut 23:3), and they produce no children in a decade.

Then the second and third blows fall together. In the final clause Naomi is not even named; she is simply "the woman," stripped of every relationship that defined her. No husband to provide, no sons to protect, no grandchildren to carry the name. The line of Elimelech appears extinguished, a family erased in a foreign land.

Humanly speaking, this is a dead end. Yet God characteristically works through human emptiness, weakness and impossibility, so that the redemption that follows will be unmistakably his doing and his glory.

Was it wrong to marry Moabite women? The law forbade marriage with the Canaanites (Deut 7:3), not expressly with Moabites, but it warned of foreign wives turning hearts to their gods (1 Kgs 11:1–2). The real issue was faith: Orpah went back to her gods (v. 15); Ruth turned to the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–18 — The Crossroads: Orpah's Return and Ruth's Vow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hearing that the LORD has visited his people with bread, Naomi sets out for Bethlehem and urges both daughters-in-law to go back. Orpah, after weeping, returns; Ruth clings to Naomi and binds herself by oath to Naomi's people and Naomi's God.
verseByVerse.theology: This section turns on hesed. Naomi invokes it as a prayer over her daughters-in-law (v. 8), and Ruth embodies it in her vow: grace producing faith, and faith producing costly loyalty.
verseByVerse.examples: The fork in the road tests every relationship. Orpah's choice is reasonable by ordinary standards; Ruth's is extravagant and risky. Covenant love is proven not when staying is easy but when leaving would be sensible. Ruth shows a discipleship that counts the cost and follows anyway, the kind Jesus would later ask of his followers, and she can choose it because the God whose hesed she has seen in Naomi's house has first drawn her to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she arose with her daughters-in-law to return from the country of Moab, for she had heard in the fields of Moab that the LORD had visited his people and given them food. So she set out from the place where she was with her two daughters-in-law, and they went on the way to return to the land of Judah. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first ray of light breaks through: after the long famine, God has acted. The verb "visited" (paqad) is rich with covenant warmth; it is used when God remembers his promises and intervenes in mercy.

Naomi "arose to return," and return (shub) dominates the chapter, carrying the double sense of homecoming and repentance. The report reaches her "in the fields of Moab": God's mercy to Bethlehem reaches into exile to draw his people home. The same harvest that feeds Bethlehem will, in chapter 2, bring Ruth to the field of Boaz. Providence is already in motion. Naomi sees only the long, sorrowful road back to a hometown she left full and returns to empty; God is leading her, and her unlikely companion, into the center of his purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: But Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go, return each of you to her mother's house. May the LORD deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me. The LORD grant that you may find rest, each of you in the house of her husband!" Then she kissed them, and they lifted up their voices and wept. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi's first recorded words are a blessing, and they reveal a heart that, despite its bitterness, still believes in the LORD's goodness toward others. "May the LORD deal kindly with you" uses hesed: she prays that God's hesed will reward the hesed her daughters-in-law have shown to the dead and to her. Her prayer that they find "rest" in a husband's house is a prayer for remarriage, a widow's only earthly hope of stability.

Desolate herself, she urges away the only companions she has left, seeking their good above her own comfort. She still believes that God is kind, even though she can no longer feel that he is kind to her. And her prayer for "rest" is more prophetic than she knows: God will grant it in a way that draws one of these women deeper into the covenant, and into the line of the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to her, "No, we will return with you to your people." But Naomi said, "Turn back, my daughters; why will you go with me? Have I yet sons in my womb that they may become your husbands? Turn back, my daughters; go your way, for I am too old to have a husband. If I should say I have hope, even if I should have a husband this night and should bear sons, would you therefore wait till they were grown? Would you therefore refrain from marrying? No, my daughters, for it is exceedingly bitter to me for your sake that the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi's argument rests on levirate marriage (Deut 25:5–10), by which a dead man's brother married his widow to raise up an heir. She has no more sons, is too old to bear them, and even if she could, the women could hardly wait. Her logic is airtight, and it is meant to release them from any sense of obligation.

The final clause unveils her heart: "the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." She does not blame fate or chance or Moab; she traces her suffering directly to the LORD. Naomi never doubts God's sovereignty; she struggles to reconcile it with his goodness. She is wrong that his hand is against her (the reader knows it is secretly for her), but right that his hand is in it all.

Such is the lament of faith: a wounded soul that still addresses its complaint to God, refusing to let go of him even while accusing him. There is more faith in Naomi's bitterness than in many a placid contentment.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they lifted up their voices and wept again. And Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth clung to her. And she said, "See, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and to her gods; return after your sister-in-law." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the hinge of the chapter, where two destinies divide. Both women weep, but their tears flow toward opposite ends.

We should not despise Orpah; her choice is the reasonable one, the one ninety-nine of a hundred would make. But "Ruth clung to her." The verb (dabaq) is the word of Genesis 2:24 for a man cleaving to his wife, an unbreakable, covenantal joining.

Naomi's last attempt points to Orpah, gone back "to her people and to her gods," and the phrase exposes the stakes. To return to Moab is to return to Chemosh, Moab’s god; to stay with Naomi is to embrace the LORD. Orpah chose the safe and calculable; Ruth chose the costly, all-in commitment of faith, the faith God gives that will lose everything to gain the one thing needful.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ruth said, "Do not urge me to leave you or to return from following you. For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried. May the LORD do so to me and more also if anything but death parts me from you." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
These words are the spiritual summit of the chapter, rising line upon line in total surrender. She binds herself not only to a person but to a people and, supremely, to a God. "Your God my God" is the moment of conversion: a Moabite raised on Chemosh casts herself wholly upon the LORD.

She seals it with an oath in that God's name, "May the LORD do so to me and more also," the strongest kind of oath: she calls down God’s judgment on herself if she breaks it. Her confession is the more astonishing because she follows a bitter, empty old woman toward uncertainty, renouncing her own future. This is hesed in its purest human form, mirroring the hesed of God himself, and it anticipates the gospel: the Gentile outsider drawn by grace into the covenant, firstfruits of the nations who will say of Israel's God, "This is God, our God forever and ever" (Ps 48:14).

These words are often read at weddings. They were spoken by a daughter-in-law to her mother-in-law, not by a bride; but they describe the costly, lifelong loyalty marriage requires, so the use is a fair one by application.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Naomi saw that she was determined to go with her, she said no more. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A single quiet verse closes the great scene. Naomi, who had argued so strenuously, falls silent. "Determined" suggests Ruth had braced herself, made herself strong, set her face like flint. There is no more arguing with such resolve.

The silence may carry a trace of Naomi's numbness, perhaps even resentment of one more mouth to feed. Yet it also marks acceptance: the bond between these two women is now sealed. What Naomi cannot yet grasp is that the companion she could not dissuade is the one God will use to fill her emptiness, the great-grandmother of King David. Ruth's loyalty, received in silence, will prove the answer to a prayer Naomi could not even bring herself to pray.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–22 — Empty in Bethlehem, Yet the Harvest Begins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem to a stir of recognition. Naomi renames herself Mara: she went out full, but the LORD has brought her back empty. Yet the chapter ends with a hinge of hope: the beginning of the barley harvest.
verseByVerse.theology: Naomi brings her wound to God rather than away from him. Her lament is faith, though her reading of it is incomplete, and the closing note of barley harvest is the quiet voice of providence.
verseByVerse.examples: Naomi says her grief aloud, to God and to her neighbours, and Scripture keeps her words; a church that makes room for lament is following her example. And the barley harvest is a reminder that the seasons of God's mercy often begin precisely when our hope is at its lowest.

verseByVerse.quote: So the two of them went on until they came to Bethlehem. And when they came to Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them. And the women said, "Is this Naomi?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole town is "stirred," a buzzing ripple of astonishment. "Is this Naomi?" The woman who left a decade ago, wife and mother in a prosperous Ephrathite family, returns aged by sorrow, accompanied only by a Moabite widow. The years and the losses are written on her face. Here is the small town that remembers, the recognition that is half-disbelief, and the way suffering can change a person until old neighbors scarcely know her.

Naomi returns empty-handed just as the harvest is returning. The community's astonished question sets up Naomi's bitter reply, in which she will rename herself after her suffering. But the reader, standing at the threshold of the harvest, senses what Naomi cannot: the homecoming that looks like the end of a tragedy is the opening of redemption's work.

verseByVerse.quote: She said to them, "Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me. I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi, when the LORD has testified against me and the Almighty has brought calamity upon me?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Naomi's great lament. She rejects "Naomi" (pleasant) for "Mara" (bitter). Four times in two verses she names God as the author of her affliction, Shaddai twice and the LORD twice. This is no atheist's complaint but the lament of a believer who knows nothing happens outside God's hand; she never imagines him absent or powerless.

Yet her conclusion is mistaken: she reads her emptiness as God's verdict against her ("the LORD has testified against me"). And the irony is that she says she returned "empty" while Ruth, soon to be mother of the line of David, stands beside her. The person through whom God will fill her again is the one she does not count.

We are poor judges of our own circumstances, calling "bitter" a providence that is sweet beyond imagining. Naomi's lament is honest, and God can bear it; but it is not the last word.
verseByVerse.note: “Naomi” means “pleasant”; “Mara” means “bitter” (ESV notes). “The Almighty” is Shaddai.

verseByVerse.quote: So Naomi returned, and Ruth the Moabite her daughter-in-law with her, who returned from the country of Moab. And they came to Bethlehem at the beginning of barley harvest. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with a verse that seems merely to summarize but in fact turns the whole story toward hope.

The narrator pointedly calls Ruth "the Moabite," a reminder of her outsider status that will recur through the book, making her inclusion all the more astonishing. She "returned" from Moab, though she had never been to Bethlehem: the return of faith, a soul's homecoming to the people and God of the covenant.

Then the hinge: "the beginning of barley harvest," in spring. Just as Naomi declares herself empty, the fields are filling with grain, and into those fields Ruth will go to glean in chapter 2, the fields of a man named Boaz. Naomi sees only emptiness; God has scheduled the harvest. The chapter of emptying ends with the first sheaf of fullness ripening in the sun.

1.theology:
The Sovereignty of God in Suffering. Naomi traces every loss directly to the hand of the LORD and the Almighty (vv. 13, 20–21). The book never suggests God is absent from the tragedy; he governs it. Naomi's error is to conclude that God's sovereign hand in her suffering means his heart is against her, and the narrator quietly corrects this by the closing note of harvest. What Romans 8:28 promises is already happening in this chapter, long before Naomi can see it: the God who empties is preparing to fill, working all things, even the deaths in Moab, toward a redemption that reaches to the manger of Bethlehem.

Hesed: Steadfast Covenant Love. Hesed is the word for God’s own covenant faithfulness, a love that stays loyal and gives more than duty strictly demands. Ruth's hesed toward Naomi (vv. 16–17) mirrors God's toward his people.

The Conversion of the Outsider. Ruth's "your God my God" is one of the great conversions of the Old Testament. A Moabite, from a people barred from the assembly (Deut 23:3), casts herself on the LORD by sheer grace, an early sign of the gospel reaching the nations.
1.examples:
Then: A widow without husband or sons was among the most vulnerable people in the ancient world, economically destitute, without legal standing or future. Naomi's despair was not exaggerated. Ruth's decision to follow her meant choosing that same poverty and uncertainty in a foreign land over the security of home.

Now: Naomi warns us against reading our circumstances too soon as God's final verdict. Ruth models the all-in commitment of faith, choosing loyal love over self-protection; in an age that prizes keeping our options open, her ‘where you go I will go’ shows us that following Christ is a binding, lifelong commitment. That loyalty is not summoned by willpower: it answers a God whose steadfast love came first, and it is the fruit his Spirit now grows in his people (Gal 5:22). If you are reading this freshly bereaved, or after years of hoping for a child who has not come, Naomi’s words are in Scripture so that you may say yours: God is not offended by an honest cry. And her conclusion that the LORD was against her was not the last word. The Son of David who came from this family took the real forsakenness on the cross (Mark 15:34), so that nothing, not even death, can separate God’s people from his love (Rom 8:31–39).

2.title: Under His Wings
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Naomi had a relative of her husband's, a worthy man of the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz.<sup>2</sup>And Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, "Let me go to the field and glean among the ears of grain after him in whose sight I shall find favor." And she said to her, "Go, my daughter."<sup>3</sup>So she set out and went and gleaned in the field after the reapers, and she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who was of the clan of Elimelech.<sup>4</sup>And behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem. And he said to the reapers, "The LORD be with you!" And they answered, "The LORD bless you."<sup>5</sup>Then Boaz said to his young man who was in charge of the reapers, "Whose young woman is this?"<sup>6</sup>And the servant who was in charge of the reapers answered, "She is the young Moabite woman, who came back with Naomi from the country of Moab.<sup>7</sup>She said, 'Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves after the reapers.' So she came, and she has continued from early morning until now, except for a short rest."<sup>8</sup>Then Boaz said to Ruth, "Now, listen, my daughter, do not go to glean in another field or leave this one, but keep close to my young women.<sup>9</sup>Let your eyes be on the field that they are reaping, and go after them. Have I not charged the young men not to touch you? And when you are thirsty, go to the vessels and drink what the young men have drawn."<sup>10</sup>Then she fell on her face, bowing to the ground, and said to him, "Why have I found favor in your eyes, that you should take notice of me, since I am a foreigner?"<sup>11</sup>But Boaz answered her, "All that you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband has been fully told to me, and how you left your father and mother and your native land and came to a people that you did not know before.<sup>12</sup>The LORD repay you for what you have done, and a full reward be given you by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge!"<sup>13</sup>Then she said, "I have found favor in your eyes, my lord, for you have comforted me and spoken kindly to your servant, though I am not one of your servants."<sup>14</sup>And at mealtime Boaz said to her, "Come here and eat some bread and dip your morsel in the wine." So she sat beside the reapers, and he passed to her roasted grain. And she ate until she was satisfied, and she had some left over.<sup>15</sup>When she rose to glean, Boaz instructed his young men, saying, "Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not reproach her.<sup>16</sup>And also pull out some from the bundles for her and leave it for her to glean, and do not rebuke her."<sup>17</sup>So she gleaned in the field until evening.
