2.overview:
Chapter 2 moves from the dark interiors of grief into the open fields under the spring sun, and the whole atmosphere lifts. Ruth, the destitute foreigner, goes out to glean, the right of the poor under Israel's law. It is hard, humbling, hand-to-mouth labor, and into this ordinary scene God weaves an extraordinary providence: she "happened" to come to the field of Boaz (2:3).

Boaz is "a worthy man" (2:1), a man of substance and integrity, and a relative of Elimelech. His first words in his field are a blessing. He protects Ruth, provides for her, eats with her, and quietly has his workers leave extra grain for her to find. He goes far beyond the requirements of the law, and his generosity reveals the heart of God, which always gives more than is required.

The jewel of the chapter is Boaz's blessing in verse 12, on the God of Israel "under whose wings you have come to take refuge," a prayer he will himself become the answer to. Behind Boaz's open hand is the open hand of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Ruth Goes Out to Glean
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Boaz is introduced as a worthy relative of Elimelech. Ruth asks to glean, and 'happens' to come to the portion belonging to Boaz.
verseByVerse.theology: Providence is the book's engine, and it runs through people: Ruth's initiative, Naomi's consent, and a worthy man already standing in the right field.
verseByVerse.examples: Ruth does not sit passively waiting for provision; she goes out to hard, humble labor. Yet her diligence and God's providence are not in competition: she works, and God guides her steps. Believers labor faithfully in the ordinary, not to secure God's care but because they already rest in it, trusting that he governs the 'chances' that shape our lives.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Naomi had a relative of her husband's, a worthy man of the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator steps aside to plant a seed of hope in the reader's mind before Naomi or Ruth knows of it. The relative (moda) is a known kinsman, and crucially "of the clan of Elimelech." The careful reader, who knows that Israel’s law let a near relative redeem (rescue) a family in need, immediately senses possibility.

"A worthy man" is gibbor hayil, the term used of mighty warriors and men of valor, here denoting wealth, standing and sterling character. And his name is given at last: Boaz, the strong redeemer the story needs.

The narrator introduces Boaz to us while leaving the characters in the dark, so that we watch the unfolding providence with eyes they do not yet have. God has already positioned the answer before the need is felt, and the worthy man at the center of it points beyond himself to the Redeemer who is strength and worth itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, "Let me go to the field and glean among the ears of grain after him in whose sight I shall find favor." And she said to her, "Go, my daughter." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again she is "Ruth the Moabite," the outsider's label kept before us so that the grace shown to her lands with full force. And it is Ruth, not Naomi, who takes the initiative; Naomi remains passive in her grief.

Gleaning was the law's provision for the poor, the widow, the orphan and the sojourner (Lev 19:9–10; Deut 24:19–22): landowners were forbidden to harvest the corners of their fields or gather what was dropped. It was honest but humble labor, and not without danger for a vulnerable foreign woman.

Ruth hopes to glean "after him in whose sight I shall find favor." "Favor" (hen) is the language of grace, undeserved kindness. She knows she has no claim; she can only hope to find grace. She does not presume; she labors and trusts. Naomi's "Go, my daughter" is the first warm word she has spoken since her lament, a small thaw in the ice of her grief.

Is gleaning a model for helping the poor? The law gave the poor work, not a handout: they gathered for themselves what landowners left. As a law of the land it ended with Old Testament Israel as a nation under God’s direct rule, but its principles remain: provide for the poor with dignity and leave room for them to work (Eph 4:28; 2 Thess 3:10).
verseByVerse.note: Gleaners gathered by hand, stalk by stalk, which is why a full ephah in one day (v. 17) is remarkable.

verseByVerse.quote: So she set out and went and gleaned in the field after the reapers, and she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who was of the clan of Elimelech. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verse's power lies in deliberate understatement. "She happened to come" is in Hebrew literally "her chance chanced upon" the field of Boaz. The narrator uses the language of pure coincidence with a twinkle in his eye, for we have just been told that Boaz is a worthy kinsman of Elimelech, and now Ruth "just happens" to wander into his field, out of all the fields around Bethlehem.

The event most plainly arranged by God in the whole story is told in the language of accident, precisely to teach that in God's universe there is no such thing as chance. God's hand is not less present in the ordinary and apparently random than in the spectacular miracle; indeed, it is most often through unremarked 'coincidences' that he accomplishes his greatest purposes. Ruth thinks she is making an arbitrary choice of field; God is leading her by the hand to her redeemer. There are no random fields in the kingdom of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Boaz arrives and greets his workers with a blessing. Noticing Ruth, he learns who she is and shows her extraordinary kindness: protection, water, a noonday meal, and deliberate provision of extra grain. He blesses her for her loyalty to Naomi and prays that the God under whose wings she has taken refuge will fully reward her.
verseByVerse.theology: Boaz embodies grace that goes beyond law (v. 16), and his blessing in v. 12 gives one of Scripture's tenderest images of God as a sheltering refuge.
verseByVerse.examples: Boaz models faith that saturates daily work. His first words to his laborers are a benediction; he treats a destitute foreign woman with dignity, generosity and protection. Piety is not confined to the temple but overflows into the field and the treatment of the vulnerable. God's care for the poor usually arrives through someone's hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem. And he said to the reapers, "The LORD be with you!" And they answered, "The LORD bless you." Then Boaz said to his young man who was in charge of the reapers, "Whose young woman is this?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And behold": at the moment Ruth is gleaning, Boaz himself comes from Bethlehem. The providence that brought Ruth to this field now brings its owner to her.

What are the first words out of Boaz's mouth? "The LORD be with you!", a blessing on his workers. And they answer in kind: "The LORD bless you." This brief exchange tells us everything about the spiritual climate of Boaz's household.

In the days when "everyone did what was right in his own eyes," here is a man whose faith flows naturally into his speech and his dealings with his laborers. His godliness is most visible where it is hardest to sustain: in the rough world of business and labor.

Then he notices the newcomer. In that culture a woman belonged to a household, and "Whose young woman is this?" is the proper inquiry of a responsible man. It is also the question that opens the door to everything that follows: the redeemer has caught sight of the woman he will redeem.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant who was in charge of the reapers answered, "She is the young Moabite woman, who came back with Naomi from the country of Moab. She said, 'Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves after the reapers.' So she came, and she has continued from early morning until now, except for a short rest." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The foreman testifies to two things. First, Ruth's humility: she asked permission and gleaned only "after the reapers," taking the lowest place. Second, her diligence: she has worked from early morning with only a short rest. His unprompted commendation is a character witness; the narrator builds our admiration for Ruth before Boaz's generosity descends, so that we feel her worthiness and her need together.

Ruth's faith is not passive: she trusts God, and she labors from dawn. Her hard work does not earn the grace that is coming, but it is where that grace finds her, and it has caught the attention of the God who notices the labor of the lowly and the cry of the widow and the stranger.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Boaz said to Ruth, "Now, listen, my daughter, do not go to glean in another field or leave this one, but keep close to my young women. Let your eyes be on the field that they are reaping, and go after them. Have I not charged the young men not to touch you? And when you are thirsty, go to the vessels and drink what the young men have drawn." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz's first words to Ruth are tender and protective: "my daughter." Though they will later marry, here he speaks as a guardian, putting the vulnerable foreigner at ease.

His kindness is immediate and concrete. She is to stay in his field rather than wander where she might be exposed to danger, and glean alongside his young women under his household's protection. He has charged the young men not to touch her, protection from harassment or assault for a young foreign widow who was tragically vulnerable. And she may drink the water his men have drawn, treated as one of his own household.

Boaz’s protection is a picture of the way Christ shelters his own: he does not merely permit the vulnerable to come near; he actively guards them. Already, before any romance, Boaz is acting as a kind of redeemer, and the wings of refuge he will pray for in verse 12 are beginning to spread over Ruth.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she fell on her face, bowing to the ground, and said to him, "Why have I found favor in your eyes, that you should take notice of me, since I am a foreigner?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth's response is pure astonishment at grace. She falls on her face, bowing to the ground, a posture of profound humility and gratitude.

Her question pierces to the heart of the gospel. "Favor" is hen, unmerited kindness, and "foreigner" (nokriyah) stresses her complete lack of any claim: a Moabite from a people barred from the assembly. Why should I, who have no right, be shown such kindness? Her wonder at being "noticed" is the very wonder of the redeemed soul before the grace of God, and the believer never gets over that question.

A wordplay runs through the Hebrew: "take notice" (nakar) and "foreigner" (nokriyah) share a root, so Ruth is in effect saying, "Why have you 'recognized' me, an 'unrecognizable' one?" The very thing that should have made her invisible has become the occasion for grace. Such is the scandal and glory of the gospel: God notices precisely those who have no claim.

verseByVerse.quote: But Boaz answered her, "All that you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband has been fully told to me, and how you left your father and mother and your native land and came to a people that you did not know before." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz answers that Ruth's reputation has preceded her. She stood by Naomi after her husband's death and left father, mother and native land for a people she did not know. The careful reader hears the echo of Genesis 12:1, where God called Abraham to leave "your country and your kindred and your father's house."

The allusion is deliberate: Ruth has made an Abraham-like journey of faith, leaving everything and trusting the God of Israel. She is a daughter of Abraham by faith, though not by blood, exactly the principle Paul would later expound (Gal 3:7, "it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham").

Yet we must not mistake the order: Ruth's loyalty does not earn the redemption to come; it is the fruit of the faith that has already taken hold of her. The grace that drew her to the God of Israel now flowers in the very love that Boaz commends.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD repay you for what you have done, and a full reward be given you by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the tenderest verse in the chapter. The word for "wings" is kanaf, the wing of a bird, and it pictures the Almighty God of Israel as a mother bird sheltering her young. Ruth has not merely come to Bethlehem; she has come to take refuge under the wings of the LORD. This is the heart of saving faith: fleeing to God as one's shelter.

The image runs like a golden thread through Scripture, "in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge" (Ps 57:1); "he will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge" (Ps 91:4), and it reaches its most poignant expression on the lips of Jesus weeping over Jerusalem: "How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!" (Matt 23:37).

And the wonder Boaz cannot yet see: in chapter 3 Ruth will ask him to spread his own "wings" (kanaf) over her. Boaz prays a prayer that God will answer through Boaz himself.
verseByVerse.note: “Wings” can also mean the corners of a garment (ESV note at 3:9), the same word Ruth uses to Boaz.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she said, "I have found favor in your eyes, my lord, for you have comforted me and spoken kindly to your servant, though I am not one of your servants." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth receives Boaz's blessing with grateful wonder, and her words again breathe the spirit of grace. She names the grace (hen) she had questioned in verse 10, now received. "You have comforted me" speaks of consolation in grief, comfort at last for women who returned in sorrow. "You have spoken kindly" is literally "you have spoken to the heart," an idiom for tenderness and reassurance.

Then the crowning humility: "though I am not one of your servants." She has no standing in his household and no claim on his kindness, and so his grace astonishes her the more. That is the perpetual posture of the redeemed: dignity in humility, neither grovelling nor presuming, receiving with open hands what she has not earned. Boaz's kind words have done what no mere provision of grain could do: they have comforted a grieving heart and made an outsider feel, for the first time since her losses, that she has found a place of welcome. This is the comfort of the gospel in miniature: to be spoken to tenderly by the one who has every right to ignore us.

verseByVerse.quote: And at mealtime Boaz said to her, "Come here and eat some bread and dip your morsel in the wine." So she sat beside the reapers, and he passed to her roasted grain. And she ate until she was satisfied, and she had some left over. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz's kindness now becomes table fellowship, and in the ancient world to share a meal was to extend belonging. The foreign gleaner eats with his own reapers, and the master of the field passes her roasted grain with his own hand, personal attention to a nobody.

"She ate until she was satisfied, and she had some left over": fullness, more than enough, a reversal for a woman from a household defined by emptiness and famine.

Many Christians have heard a gospel echo here: a foreigner welcomed to the table, served by the lord of the harvest, filled with provision she could never have earned. It is like a small foretaste of the great supper of the Lamb, where outsiders from every nation are gathered to a table they had no right to, served by the Lord himself, and satisfied forever. The leftover grain she will carry home to Naomi: grace, when it comes, comes in baskets that overflow.

verseByVerse.quote: When she rose to glean, Boaz instructed his young men, saying, "Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not reproach her. And also pull out some from the bundles for her and leave it for her to glean, and do not rebuke her." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here Boaz's grace soars past every legal requirement, in private instructions Ruth herself does not hear.

The gleaning law permitted the poor to gather only from the corners and what was dropped (Lev 19:9–10); Boaz lets Ruth glean "even among the sheaves," where gleaners were never normally allowed, and has his men deliberately drop extra grain where she will find it. Twice he charges them not to reproach her.

Here is the heart of the chapter's theology. The law set a floor for provision; Boaz's grace knows no ceiling, and he gives secretly, so that she experiences it simply as the bounty of the field. The older English versions caught the phrase beautifully: "handfuls of purpose for her" (Ruth 2:16, KJV). That is how the grace of God works. He does not deal with us according to the strict requirements of the law; he orders our circumstances so that grace overflows where we least expect it, leaving handfuls on purpose for us to find. Behind the unexpected provisions and undeserved kindnesses that meet us is a Redeemer who has quietly arranged the circumstances of our lives to bless us beyond all law and merit.

verseByVerse.quote: So she gleaned in the field until evening. Then she beat out what she had gleaned, and it was about an ephah of barley. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth gleaned from early morning (v. 7) until evening, and when she beat out what she had gleaned, the yield was about an ephah of barley, some thirty pounds of grain, enough to feed two women for many days, perhaps weeks. For an ordinary gleaner such a harvest in a single day would have been extraordinary; it is Boaz's secret generosity, the handfuls on purpose, now weighed out in the basket.

The narrator lets the abundance speak. Ruth set out hoping merely to glean enough to keep two widows alive; she returns staggering under a harvest of plenty. The contrast with chapter 1 is deliberate: the God who emptied Naomi (1:21) is beginning, through the kindness of Boaz, to fill her again, through the most ordinary means, a day's honest labor blessed by hidden grace. The God of providence often pours out his most lavish gifts through the most mundane channels. Ruth's basket is heavy with more than grain; it is heavy with the dawning of redemption.
verseByVerse.note: An ephah was about 3/5 bushel (ESV note), far more than a gleaner could expect.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ruth brings the abundant grain home, and Naomi learns that the man who showed such kindness is Boaz, 'one of our redeemers.' For the first time Naomi speaks of the LORD's kindness, and her bitterness begins to thaw. Ruth gleans on through the barley and wheat harvests.
verseByVerse.theology: The key word emerges: go'el, kinsman-redeemer. Naomi recognizes Boaz as 'one of our redeemers' (v. 20), and for the first time since her lament she calls on the LORD to bless, declaring that his hesed has not forsaken the living or the dead. The hidden providence of chapter 1 is becoming visible.
verseByVerse.examples: Bitterness rarely yields to argument. It often begins to thaw when someone's practical kindness becomes evidence of God's, as a basket of barley did for Naomi.

verseByVerse.quote: And she took it up and went into the city. Her mother-in-law saw what she had gleaned. She also brought out and gave her what food she had left over after being satisfied. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth carries the heavy ephah back into the city, and Naomi sees what she has gleaned. We can imagine the astonishment on the old woman's face; such a quantity from a single day could only mean that something remarkable had happened in the field.

Before Naomi can even ask, Ruth gives her what food she had left over after being satisfied (v. 14). She did not consume it or hoard it; she carried it home. Even the abundance she received at Boaz's table becomes provision for the mother-in-law she vowed to serve. Grace received always overflows in grace given; the one who has been filled cannot help but share. Ruth's hesed toward Naomi continues unabated: she labors all day, saves some of her meal, and brings the surplus home. The destitute foreigner is feeding the Israelite widow, and Naomi, who called herself "empty," sees the evidence of returning fullness carried through her door by the daughter-in-law she once tried to send away.

verseByVerse.quote: And her mother-in-law said to her, "Where did you glean today? And where have you worked? Blessed be the man who took notice of you." So she told her mother-in-law with whom she had worked and said, "The man's name with whom I worked today is Boaz." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The abundance prompts Naomi's eager questions, and before she learns the name she blesses the man who "took notice" (nakar) of Ruth, the same Hebrew word Ruth used in verse 10. Such a harvest could only come from extraordinary kindness.

Then the dramatic revelation, delivered with careful timing: "The man's name with whom I worked today is Boaz." The narrator's skill lies in withholding and then releasing the information, and the name lands with its full weight. The reader has known since verse 1 that he is a kinsman of Elimelech and has waited for this recognition. What Ruth experienced as the kindness of a generous stranger, Naomi will recognize as the hand of God, and the man Ruth happened upon as the man positioned by heaven to redeem them. Hope, long dead in Naomi's heart, is about to draw its first breath.

verseByVerse.quote: And Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, "May he be blessed by the LORD, whose kindness has not forsaken the living or the dead!" Naomi also said to her, "The man is a close relative of ours, one of our redeemers." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse marks the turning of Naomi's soul. In 1:20–21 she said the Almighty had dealt bitterly with her; now she blesses the LORD, "whose kindness has not forsaken the living or the dead!"

"Kindness" is hesed. The woman who felt abandoned by God now perceives that his steadfast love has never let go of her family, whether the living (herself and Ruth) or the dead (Elimelech and her sons, whose line may yet be preserved).

Then the pivotal word of the book: Boaz is "one of our redeemers," a go'el. Under Israel's law the go'el was a near relative with the right and responsibility to rescue a family member in distress: to buy back land sold in poverty (Lev 25:25), to redeem a relative sold into slavery (Lev 25:47–49), to avenge a slain kinsman (Num 35:19), and, by extension, to marry a childless widow and raise up an heir for the dead.

The go’el is a pattern that Christ fulfils. He became our near kinsman by taking our flesh and blood (Heb 2:14–17), and who has the right, the resources, and the willingness to redeem his people. In Boaz, God has provided a redeemer, and the empty woman has been given a future.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew word is go'el. Boaz is "one of" Naomi's redeemers, and there is a nearer one (3:12).

verseByVerse.quote: And Ruth the Moabite said, "Besides, he said to me, 'You shall keep close by my young men until they have finished all my harvest.'" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth, still "the Moabite" even as redemption dawns, adds a detail she had not reported: she may keep close to Boaz's workers "until they have finished all my harvest." Her gleaning is not a single day's mercy but security for the whole barley and wheat harvests, several weeks of guaranteed provision. As Ruth reports it, Boaz said "keep close by my young men" (in v. 8 he had said "my young women"), which Naomi will gently amend in the next verse for Ruth's protection.

This is not a one-time handout but a standing promise of provision. The cumulative weight of Boaz's kindnesses, protection, water, a meal, extra grain, and now season-long welcome, builds a portrait of generosity far beyond duty. Ruth, in her innocent reporting, does not yet see where it is leading; she simply rejoices in the practical security. Naomi sees the larger pattern. The redeemer means to sustain them through the whole harvest, and in that provision the seed of a far greater redemption is germinating.

verseByVerse.quote: And Naomi said to Ruth, her daughter-in-law, "It is good, my daughter, that you go out with his young women, lest in another field you be assaulted." So she kept close to the young women of Boaz, gleaning until the end of the barley and wheat harvests. And she lived with her mother-in-law. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi, alert now where before she was passive in grief, gives protective counsel: Ruth should stay with "his young women," safer company for a vulnerable foreign widow, "lest in another field you be assaulted." Her renewed concern shows how fully her heart has reengaged with life and hope; the woman who once urged Ruth away now plans carefully for her good.

The summary spans the barley and wheat harvests, about seven weeks of Ruth's daily labor and Boaz's daily provision. And "she lived with her mother-in-law": Ruth did not drift away once provision was secured; she remained faithful to her vow.

This closing line of stability and loyalty sets the stage for chapter 3, where the question shifts from daily bread to permanent rest, from gleaning to redemption. The harvest is gathered, the redeemer identified, and the two faithful women dwell together in hope. The narrator has filled the empty barns and the empty hearts; now he will fill the empty future.
verseByVerse.note: Barley and wheat harvests together ran about seven weeks, from Passover to Pentecost.

2.theology:
The Hidden Providence of God. Chapter 2 shows how God's sovereignty ordinarily operates: not chiefly through spectacular miracle but through 'coincidence' and the faithful obedience of ordinary people (v. 3). What Ruth experiences as chance is the orchestration of a sovereign Lord who has already positioned her redeemer (v. 1).

Grace Beyond Law. The gleaning laws set a floor of provision for the poor; Boaz has grain pulled from the bundles and left for her on purpose (v. 16). God does not deal with his people according to strict legal measure but pours out abundance we could never earn.

The Refuge of God's Wings. Boaz's blessing in v. 12 presents God as a sheltering mother bird, and this is the picture of saving faith: fleeing to God for refuge. The image culminates on the lips of Jesus, who longed to gather Jerusalem 'as a hen gathers her brood under her wings' (Matt 23:37).
2.examples:
Then: Gleaning was Israel's social safety net for the poor, the widow, the orphan and the foreigner, a divinely mandated provision that required landowners to leave the edges of their fields, and whatever the reapers dropped, for the destitute. Boaz's protection of Ruth, his water and food, and his extra grain all went far beyond what the law required, modeling the heart of God toward the marginalized.

Now: Begin where Ruth began, with her wonder: 'Why have I found favor in your eyes?' Grace found us when we had no claim, and Christ our Redeemer has given us far more than any law required. Out of that, Boaz shows us faith filling ordinary work and business. Godliness is most credible where it is hardest: in the marketplace, and in our treatment of those who can do nothing for us. The Spirit who has made us God's own makes us his 'handfuls on purpose' in the fields of a hurting world, for the hidden providence of God so often reaches the vulnerable through the open hands of his people.

3.title: The Bold Request
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Naomi her mother-in-law said to her, "My daughter, should I not seek rest for you, that it may be well with you?<sup>2</sup>Is not Boaz our relative, with whose young women you were? See, he is winnowing barley tonight at the threshing floor.<sup>3</sup>Wash therefore and anoint yourself, and put on your cloak and go down to the threshing floor, but do not make yourself known to the man until he has finished eating and drinking.<sup>4</sup>But when he lies down, observe the place where he lies. Then go and uncover his feet and lie down, and he will tell you what to do."<sup>5</sup>And she replied, "All that you say I will do."<sup>6</sup>So she went down to the threshing floor and did just as her mother-in-law had commanded her.<sup>7</sup>And when Boaz had eaten and drunk, and his heart was merry, he went to lie down at the end of the heap of grain. Then she came softly and uncovered his feet and lay down.<sup>8</sup>At midnight the man was startled and turned over, and behold, a woman lay at his feet!<sup>9</sup>He said, "Who are you?" And she answered, "I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer."<sup>10</sup>And he said, "May you be blessed by the LORD, my daughter. You have made this last kindness greater than the first in that you have not gone after young men, whether poor or rich.<sup>11</sup>And now, my daughter, do not fear. I will do for you all that you ask, for all my fellow townsmen know that you are a worthy woman.<sup>12</sup>And now it is true that I am a redeemer. Yet there is a redeemer nearer than I.<sup>13</sup>Remain tonight, and in the morning, if he will redeem you, good; let him do it. But if he is not willing to redeem you, then, as the LORD lives, I will redeem you. Lie down until the morning."<sup>14</sup>So she lay at his feet until the morning, but arose before one could recognize another. And he said, "Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor."<sup>15</sup>And he said, "Bring the garment you are wearing and hold it out." So she held it, and he measured out six measures of barley and put it on her. Then she went into the city.<sup>16</sup>And when she came to her mother-in-law, she said, "How did you fare, my daughter?" Then she told her all that the man had done for her,<sup>17</sup>saying, "These six measures of barley he gave to me, for he said to me, 'You must not go back empty-handed to your mother-in-law.'"<sup>18</sup>She replied, "Wait, my daughter, until you learn how the matter turns out, for the man will not rest but will settle the matter today."
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the daring heart of the book, a scene charged with tension, tenderness and theological weight. The harvests are over, and with them the temporary provision of gleaning. Naomi, revived from her bitterness and thinking once more like a mother, conceives a bold and risky plan to secure for Ruth not merely bread but "rest," a home and a permanent future (3:1). She sends Ruth by night to the threshing floor where Boaz will be sleeping.

The scene is morally delicate: a woman approaching a man at night and lying down at his feet. Yet the narrator presents both Ruth and Boaz as people of sterling integrity. Ruth's request is not seduction but a marriage proposal in the language of covenant and redemption (3:9).

Boaz responds without offense, exploitation or self-interest. He blesses her, calls her a "worthy woman" (3:11), matching the "worthy man" he himself was called in 2:1, and commits himself to redeem her. But a nearer kinsman has the prior right (3:12), and Boaz, scrupulously just, will not act outside the proper order. He sends Ruth home before dawn with a generous gift of grain and a promise to settle the matter that very day.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the harvest ended, Naomi devises a plan for Ruth's permanent security. Ruth is to wash, anoint herself, dress well, and go secretly to the threshing floor at night, lie at Boaz's feet and let him direct what follows. Ruth agrees.
verseByVerse.theology: The plan, culturally bold and morally precarious, aims to invoke the law of the kinsman-redeemer to secure Ruth's future and preserve Elimelech's line. Naomi's change from despairing widow to active matchmaker shows faith beginning to hope and act again.
verseByVerse.examples: Naomi seeks not merely Ruth's survival but her flourishing, not just bread but a home. Genuine love looks beyond immediate needs to lasting good. Yet the plan carries real risk, reminding us that faithful people act within imperfect circumstances, planning wisely while the result rests in God's hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Naomi her mother-in-law said to her, "My daughter, should I not seek rest for you, that it may be well with you?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi takes the initiative, a striking contrast to the grief-stricken woman of chapter 1. "Rest" (manoah) means a settled home, security, a permanent place of belonging. It is what she prayed for in 1:9, "rest, each of you in the house of her husband," and now she sets out to become the means by which that prayer is answered, seeking that it may be "well" with Ruth.

That is what real love seeks: not the temporary relief of gleaning but the lasting security of a home. Naomi has come a long way from "call me Mara."

The "rest" Naomi seeks foreshadows the rest the gospel offers, the secure belonging that comes through redemption. As Augustine famously prayed, our hearts are restless until they find their rest in God. Naomi, perhaps without knowing it, is reaching toward the rest that redemption brings, to which the whole story is moving.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is not Boaz our relative, with whose young women you were? See, he is winnowing barley tonight at the threshing floor. Wash therefore and anoint yourself, and put on your cloak and go down to the threshing floor, but do not make yourself known to the man until he has finished eating and drinking. But when he lies down, observe the place where he lies. Then go and uncover his feet and lie down, and he will tell you what to do." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi’s plan is detailed, bold and full of meaning in that culture. Boaz is "our relative," a go'el, and will be winnowing at the threshing floor that night. There grain was separated from chaff by tossing it into the evening breeze, and landowners often slept there at harvest to guard the heaps.

"Wash... anoint yourself, and put on your cloak" suggests a woman preparing for a significant encounter, perhaps putting off the garments of mourning to present herself as a bride-to-be. Read in light of her words in verse 9, the uncovering of the feet and lying down is not seductive but a symbolic gesture inviting Boaz to extend his protection.

"He will tell you what to do": Naomi trusts Boaz's integrity to direct the encounter rightly. The plan walks a knife's edge, and she is staking everything on the godliness of a worthy man and the providence of God.

Was “uncover his feet” sexual? Some read it as a euphemism or a seduction. But the text says feet, Boaz calls her a worthy woman (v. 11), and he sends her home before anyone sees her, protecting her name. It was a bold, unusual request for marriage, made in a way that left the decision to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And she replied, "All that you say I will do." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth's answer is complete trust and submission: "All that you say I will do." No hesitation, no objection, no calculation of the risk to her reputation or safety. The same hesed that bound her to Naomi at the crossroads now governs her willingness to follow this bold plan, a trust forged in shared suffering and sealed by covenant loyalty.

There is quiet courage here. A foreign widow with only her reputation to protect agrees to a plan that could be catastrophically misunderstood, because she trusts both Naomi and the God under whose wings she has taken refuge. Ruth's willingness to do "all" that Naomi says is the obedience of faith: stepping into a risky and unclear situation, trusting the guidance she has been given and the God who governs the outcome. She is about to walk by faith into the dark, trusting that the God of Israel will not let her fall.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ruth goes to the threshing floor and waits until Boaz lies down. At midnight he wakes, startled to find a woman at his feet. Ruth makes her bold request: 'Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer.' Boaz responds with blessing and honor, pledging to redeem her, but reveals that a nearer kinsman has the prior right.
verseByVerse.theology: Boaz is willing, but he will not cut corners: he honours the nearer kinsman's prior claim, so that redemption proceeds in righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: Character is tested where nobody is watching. Boaz had every opportunity in the dark and used none of it; he protected a vulnerable woman's honor and acted justly.

verseByVerse.quote: So she went down to the threshing floor and did just as her mother-in-law had commanded her. And when Boaz had eaten and drunk, and his heart was merry, he went to lie down at the end of the heap of grain. Then she came softly and uncovered his feet and lay down. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth carries out the plan with quiet courage. Boaz, after the labor of winnowing, eats and drinks, and "his heart was merry," the good cheer of a meal with wine, though the narrator gives no hint that he was drunk and is careful to preserve his dignity. He lies down "at the end of the heap of grain," guarding the precious harvest through the night.

"She came softly," so as not to wake him or attract notice. Every word is charged with risk; a single misstep, a single misunderstanding, could ruin Ruth's reputation and Naomi's hopes forever. The narrator holds us in suspense, but he has established the integrity of both characters. Ruth has done the bold thing faith required; now she lies in the dark and waits, her future hanging on what the worthy man will do when he wakes.

verseByVerse.quote: At midnight the man was startled and turned over, and behold, a woman lay at his feet! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
"At midnight," the deepest dark and most vulnerable hour, "the man was startled." The Hebrew suggests a sudden shudder; perhaps the night had grown cold. The narrator's "behold" lets us see it through Boaz's astonished eyes: a woman lies at his feet in the dark. The moment is full of possibility and danger. He does not know who she is or why she is there, and the situation could be interpreted in any number of ways, most of them scandalous.

This is the hinge of the chapter. How will this worthy man respond when no one is watching and he could do anything? The darkness of the threshing floor will make Ruth's faith and Boaz's righteousness shine the brighter. The question "Who are you?" will open the door to the exchange the whole book has been waiting for.

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "Who are you?" And she answered, "I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the heart of the book, and it deserves to be lingered over with wonder. Ruth's answer to "Who are you?" is a masterpiece of humble boldness.

She names herself "your servant," presuming on no status. Then the request, using kanaf, the very word of Boaz's prayer in 2:12 that the LORD, "under whose wings you have come to take refuge," would reward her. With insight and courage Ruth turns his prayer back upon him: you prayed that I would find refuge under God's wings; now spread your wing of covering over me.

To "spread one's wing" (or skirt, the corner of one's garment) over a woman was an idiom for marriage and protection (cf. Ezek 16:8). And she grounds her appeal not in her worthiness but in his role: "for you are a redeemer." You are a redeemer; therefore redeem me. This is precisely how the soul comes to Christ: not 'I am worthy,' but 'You are the Redeemer; spread your wings over me.'
verseByVerse.note: “Spread your wings” uses the word for corners of a garment (ESV note): a request for marriage and protection.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "May you be blessed by the LORD, my daughter. You have made this last kindness greater than the first in that you have not gone after young men, whether poor or rich." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz's response melts the tension and reveals a noble heart. No offense, no exploitation, no suspicion; his first instinct is to invoke God's blessing on her, tenderly, as "my daughter."

Then he honors her loyalty. "Kindness" is again hesed. The "first" was Ruth's faithfulness to Naomi in leaving her homeland; the "last" and greater is that a young woman has sought to marry an older kinsman to preserve her dead husband's line and provide for Naomi. She could easily have sought a husband among the young men of Bethlehem, poor or rich; instead she has put loyalty to Naomi’s family above her own wishes.

A lesser man might have been flattered or taken advantage; Boaz is humbled and grateful, his thought entirely for Ruth's honor and welfare. He sees her request not as forward but as the crowning act of her self-giving hesed. In a single verse a potentially scandalous midnight encounter becomes a pledge of honor and blessing. The worthy man has met the worthy woman, and grace abounds.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, my daughter, do not fear. I will do for you all that you ask, for all my fellow townsmen know that you are a worthy woman. And now it is true that I am a redeemer. Yet there is a redeemer nearer than I. Remain tonight, and in the morning, if he will redeem you, good; let him do it. But if he is not willing to redeem you, then, as the LORD lives, I will redeem you. Lie down until the morning." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz's words are a model of tenderness, integrity and resolve. "Do not fear" calms her; "I will do for you all that you ask" commits him to her cause.

"Worthy woman" (eshet hayil) is the precise counterpart to the "worthy man" (gibbor hayil) of 2:1, and the phrase that crowns the virtuous woman of Proverbs 31:10. The worthy man and the worthy woman belong together.

Then a complication that displays his justice: "there is a redeemer nearer than I." Boaz will not seize the role by bypassing the proper order. Yet his commitment is sealed with an oath: "as the LORD lives, I will redeem you" if the other will not.

The gospel echo is plain enough: there is a nearer redeemer who has the right but, as chapter 4 will show, lacks the willingness. Some Christians have seen in him a picture of the law, which has a prior claim on us, but it cannot ultimately redeem; only the willing Redeemer can. Ruth lies down until morning, safe, honored, and bound to him by promise.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ruth lies at Boaz's feet until before dawn, then rises to avoid scandal. Boaz sends her home with six measures of barley, a pledge of his intentions and a gift for Naomi. Naomi assures Ruth that Boaz will not rest until the matter is settled that very day.
verseByVerse.theology: The barley is provision and promise together, a pledge from the redeemer of what he will do.
verseByVerse.examples: Boaz's care in sending Ruth away before dawn models the care genuine love takes for the honor of the beloved, and his gift shows commitment expressed in tangible provision.

verseByVerse.quote: So she lay at his feet until the morning, but arose before one could recognize another. And he said, "Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth lies at Boaz's feet through the rest of the night, in complete propriety, and rises in the gray dawn before anyone could recognize her.

"Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor" is not the secrecy of guilt but the wisdom of honor. Boaz knows how easily this innocent encounter could be misread by gossiping tongues, and he guards Ruth's name as zealously as his own. The care also serves the larger purpose: talk of a secret night meeting could jeopardize the lawful, public redemption he intends at the city gate. So Boaz protects not only Ruth's name but the very possibility of her redemption, with a love that will not let even the appearance of evil cloud the path to a righteous union.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Bring the garment you are wearing and hold it out." So she held it, and he measured out six measures of barley and put it on her. Then she went into the city. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz pours six measures of barley into the garment Ruth holds out. The exact quantity is uncertain, but it was a generous load, heavy enough that he had to lift it onto her.

The gift is a pledge, a token of serious intent, and it ensures that Ruth will not return to Naomi empty-handed. The narrator surely intends the echo of 1:21: "I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty." The woman who declared herself empty is receiving, measure after measure, the filling of grace.

The text does not tell us why six, and guessing at the number is a distraction from what the gesture plainly is: the redeemer's gift is both provision and promise, a down payment on the full redemption to come. He gives lavishly, and he binds himself to his word with something Ruth can carry in her arms. The empty house is being filled, grain by grain, with the firstfruits of redemption.

verseByVerse.quote: And when she came to her mother-in-law, she said, "How did you fare, my daughter?" Then she told her all that the man had done for her, saying, "These six measures of barley he gave to me, for he said to me, 'You must not go back empty-handed to your mother-in-law.'" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth returns to Naomi, who greets her with an eager question, literally "Who are you, my daughter?", perhaps asked in the dim light, or more likely asking in effect, "How did it go? Are you betrothed?"

Ruth recounts all that Boaz had done and presents the barley with his own words attached: "You must not go back empty-handed to your mother-in-law." This is a precious detail: Boaz's generosity was directed not only toward Ruth but toward Naomi as well. The redeemer's care reaches the whole family: the woman who came home empty will not be left so. The God who emptied is now, through his chosen redeemer, filling.

Ruth's report is not merely a recounting of events but a proclamation of hope: the man has acted, the man has given, the man has pledged that emptiness will not have the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: She replied, "Wait, my daughter, until you learn how the matter turns out, for the man will not rest but will settle the matter today." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi's closing counsel is the perfect note on which to end the chapter: "Wait... until you learn how the matter turns out." Having done all that faith and shrewdness required, Ruth can now only rest in the redeemer's faithfulness.

Naomi's reason for confidence is a magnificent testimony to Boaz's character: "the man will not rest but will settle the matter today." Naomi knows his integrity, his resolve, his commitment. He is not the kind of man who delays or wavers or forgets; having pledged himself, he will pursue the redemption to completion that very day.

The gospel parallel is clear: the believer's rest is grounded not in his own efforts but in the unwavering commitment of the Redeemer to finish what he has begun. "He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion" (Phil 1:6). As Boaz will not rest until Ruth is redeemed, so Christ will not rest until his people are fully and finally his. A holy restlessness beats in the heart of every true redeemer, a refusal to leave the work half-done. The chapter of the bold request ends not in anxiety but in restful expectation: the redeemer is at work, and the bride waits in peace, for everything now depends on the faithfulness of the one who has pledged to redeem her.

3.theology:
The Willing Redeemer. Ruth appeals to Boaz not on the basis of her worth but of his identity: 'you are a redeemer' (v. 9). Boaz responds with blessing, honor and an unconditional pledge sealed by oath (vv. 10–13). This willingness is the heart of what the book shows us about Christ. A redeemer must have the right, the resources and the willingness to redeem. Boaz did not have to redeem Ruth; he chose to, out of love. So Christ came willingly, and it is his willingness the gospel celebrates: he loved us and gave himself for us (Gal 2:20).

Spread Your Wings: The Prayer Answered Through the Pray-er. Ruth's request (v. 9) deliberately echoes Boaz's own prayer in 2:12, and asks him to become the human means by which God answers it. God often answers our prayers for others by making us the instrument of the very blessing we requested. God shelters people under his wings through the care his obedient people give, and supremely through Christ, who gathers his own to himself.

The Posture of Saving Faith. Ruth comes in lowliness ('your servant'), in boldness ('spread your wings over me'), and in confident appeal to his role ('you are a redeemer'). This is the posture of the soul coming to Christ: not pleading our own merit but appealing to who he is, the Savior. We do not say to Christ, 'I am worthy'; we say, 'You are the Redeemer; cover me.'
3.examples:
Then: The customs of the kinsman-redeemer and levirate marriage (Lev 25:25; Deut 25:5–10) lie behind Ruth’s bold approach. Her request that Boaz spread his garment over her was a recognized idiom for marriage and protection, and both of them acted with complete integrity in a scene that could easily have caused scandal.

Now: Ruth teaches us how to come to our Redeemer: not with pride in our achievements but with the bold humility that says, 'You are the Redeemer; spread your wings over me.' We approach Christ empty-handed, appealing not to our worth but to his role and his willingness. Boaz models a love that guards the honor of the beloved, acts in righteousness rather than seizing advantage, and gives tangible pledges of commitment. And Naomi's counsel to 'wait' teaches the restful patience of faith: having done all, we trust the One who 'will not rest but will settle the matter today,' confident that he who began a good work will complete it. The chapter is not a template for night-time visits: its custom belonged to its world. What carries over is the integrity on both sides, Ruth’s bold honesty and the way Boaz guards her name.

4.title: The Redeemer Steps Forward
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Boaz had gone up to the gate and sat down there. And behold, the redeemer, of whom Boaz had spoken, came by. So Boaz said, "Turn aside, friend; sit down here." And he turned aside and sat down.<sup>2</sup>And he took ten men of the elders of the city and said, "Sit down here." So they sat down.<sup>3</sup>Then he said to the redeemer, "Naomi, who has come back from the country of Moab, is selling the parcel of land that belonged to our relative Elimelech.<sup>4</sup>So I thought I would tell you of it and say, 'Buy it in the presence of those sitting here and in the presence of the elders of my people.' If you will redeem it, redeem it. But if you will not, tell me, that I may know, for there is no one besides you to redeem it, and I come after you." And he said, "I will redeem it."<sup>5</sup>Then Boaz said, "The day you buy the field from the hand of Naomi, you also acquire Ruth the Moabite, the widow of the dead, in order to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance."<sup>6</sup>Then the redeemer said, "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance. Take my right of redemption yourself, for I cannot redeem it."<sup>7</sup>Now this was the custom in former times in Israel concerning redeeming and exchanging: to confirm a transaction, the one drew off his sandal and gave it to the other, and this was the manner of attesting in Israel.<sup>8</sup>So when the redeemer said to Boaz, "Buy it for yourself," he drew off his sandal.<sup>9</sup>Then Boaz said to the elders and all the people, "You are witnesses this day that I have bought from the hand of Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech and all that belonged to Chilion and to Mahlon.<sup>10</sup>Also Ruth the Moabite, the widow of Mahlon, I have bought to be my wife, to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance, that the name of the dead may not be cut off from among his brothers and from the gate of his native place. You are witnesses this day."<sup>11</sup>Then all the people who were at the gate and the elders said, "We are witnesses. May the LORD make the woman, who is coming into your house, like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. May you act worthily in Ephrathah and be renowned in Bethlehem,<sup>12</sup>and may your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, because of the offspring that the LORD will give you by this young woman."<sup>13</sup>So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. And he went in to her, and the LORD gave her conception, and she bore a son.<sup>14</sup>Then the women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer, and may his name be renowned in Israel!<sup>15</sup>He shall be to you a restorer of life and a nourisher of your old age, for your daughter-in-law who loves you, who is more to you than seven sons, has given birth to him."<sup>16</sup>Then Naomi took the child and laid him on her lap and became his nurse.<sup>17</sup>And the women of the neighborhood gave him a name, saying, "A son has been born to Naomi." They named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David.<sup>18</sup>Now these are the generations of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron,<sup>19</sup>Hezron fathered Ram, Ram fathered Amminadab,<sup>20</sup>Amminadab fathered Nahshon, Nahshon fathered Salmon,<sup>21</sup>Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed,<sup>22</sup>Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 brings the story to its resolution at the gate of Bethlehem, the place of legal transaction and public witness. Boaz, true to Naomi's confidence, convenes the proceedings before the elders and the people. At the center of this courtroom drama stands a contrast between two redeemers: the nearer kinsman who has the prior right but lacks the willingness, and Boaz, who steps forward with wholehearted resolve.

The nearer redeemer is willing to redeem the land until he learns that it means also marrying Ruth and raising up an heir who would carry the name of the dead and inherit the very property he sought. "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance" (4:6). The cost to himself is too great. Only a redeemer willing to bear the cost himself can save, and Boaz is that redeemer.

The sandal seals the transaction, the elders bless, and Boaz takes Ruth as his wife. Then the climactic verse, in which the LORD himself gives Ruth a son (4:13), and the women call the child a 'restorer of life' and place him in the lap of the woman who once cried 'call me Mara.'

Then the genealogy turns this village story into a turning point in the history of salvation. The child is Obed, father of Jesse, father of David, and an ancestor of David's greater Son, the Lord Jesus Christ. The barley field outside Bethlehem has led us, by hidden providence, all the way to the manger of Bethlehem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Boaz goes to the city gate and summons the nearer kinsman before ten elders. The kinsman agrees to redeem Naomi's land, until he learns that redemption includes marrying Ruth to raise up an heir for the dead, which would impair his own inheritance. He yields the right of redemption to Boaz.
verseByVerse.theology: Redemption requires not only right and resources but willingness. The nearer kinsman has the legal right and presumably the resources, but when the full cost is revealed, he will not pay it.
verseByVerse.examples: The nearer kinsman is the prudent, calculating man who weighs the cost of redemption against his own interest and finds it too high. He is not wicked; he is simply unwilling to be diminished for another's sake, and his 'I cannot... lest I impair my own inheritance' is the opposite of the gospel’s self-giving love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Boaz had gone up to the gate and sat down there. And behold, the redeemer, of whom Boaz had spoken, came by. So Boaz said, "Turn aside, friend; sit down here." And he turned aside and sat down. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
True to Naomi's word, Boaz goes up to the gate, the public square inside the walls where legal business and judicial matters were conducted. He does everything openly, in proper order, before legitimate witnesses.

Again the narrator's "behold" signals providence: the redeemer comes by at precisely the right moment. As with Ruth's arrival in Boaz's field (2:3), the timing is no accident.

"Friend" renders a curious idiom (peloni almoni), something like "so-and-so," a deliberate way of leaving the man unnamed. The man who would not bear the cost to preserve the name of the dead is himself left nameless in the record, while Boaz and Ruth are honored forever. A quiet justice runs through this anonymity.
verseByVerse.note: The city gate was the place of public business and law.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took ten men of the elders of the city and said, "Sit down here." So they sat down. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz convenes a formal legal assembly of ten elders. Elders served as witnesses and judges for important transactions, and ten appears to have been the recognized number needed (a tradition that continued into later Jewish practice as the minyan).

Boaz is meticulous. He assembles legitimate witnesses so that whatever is decided will be binding, public and beyond dispute, as befits a man who does things rightly throughout the book. It also serves Ruth: her redemption must be beyond challenge, so that the marriage and the child to come will be fully legitimate. His attention to legal form is itself a kind of love, securing Ruth's status and her child's. There is no cutting of corners; the redeemer wants the redemption complete and legally airtight.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the redeemer, "Naomi, who has come back from the country of Moab, is selling the parcel of land that belonged to our relative Elimelech. So I thought I would tell you of it and say, 'Buy it in the presence of those sitting here and in the presence of the elders of my people.' If you will redeem it, redeem it. But if you will not, tell me, that I may know, for there is no one besides you to redeem it, and I come after you." And he said, "I will redeem it." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz begins not with Ruth but with the land: Naomi is selling (or offering for redemption) a parcel that belonged to Elimelech. Under the law of redemption (Lev 25:25), the nearest kinsman had the right and duty to buy back family land to keep it within the clan.

Boaz scrupulously honors the man's prior claim: "there is no one besides you to redeem it, and I come after you." He could have schemed to bypass the nearer kinsman, but his integrity will not permit it.

Hearing only of the land, a profitable acquisition that would enlarge his holdings, the kinsman readily agrees: "I will redeem it." At this point it looks like a straightforward gain. The narrator withholds the crucial condition, so that the man commits himself before he learns the full cost. Boaz has arranged it so: first the man's willingness regarding the land, then the burden that comes attached. The man who will redeem for gain is about to discover that true redemption costs more than he is willing to pay.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Boaz said, "The day you buy the field from the hand of Naomi, you also acquire Ruth the Moabite, the widow of the dead, in order to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Boaz reveals the full cost. To redeem the land is also to acquire Ruth the Moabite, the widow of the dead, to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance. Land redemption (Lev 25) here meets the principle of levirate marriage (Deut 25:5–10): the redeemer must marry Ruth and raise up a son who will carry Mahlon’s name, inherit his property, and so continue Elimelech’s line.

That transforms the transaction. The land would not become a permanent addition to the redeemer's estate; the firstborn son of his union with Ruth would inherit it as the heir of the dead. He would bear the redemption price and the cost of supporting Ruth and the child, and the land would pass to that child's line, not enrich his own. And once more she is "Ruth the Moabite," the outsider label persisting to the end, making her inclusion in the line of David all the more a wonder of grace.

Redemption that costs nothing is no redemption at all. The true price is about to expose the difference between a redeemer who calculates and a redeemer who loves.

The levirate law applied to a dead man’s brother (Deut 25:5–10). Here its purpose, to preserve the dead man’s name and inheritance, is carried to the nearest kinsman, along with the redemption of the land (Lev 25:25).
verseByVerse.note: The Masoretic Text reads “you also buy it from Ruth” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the redeemer said, "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance. Take my right of redemption yourself, for I cannot redeem it." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the great refusal. His reasoning is entirely self-protective: to redeem Ruth and raise up an heir for the dead would diminish his own estate and complicate his own family's inheritance. He is not portrayed as wicked, merely prudent and unwilling to be diminished for another's sake. He surrenders his claim, and steps out of the story forever, nameless.

Many preachers have drawn a lesson from this moment, though the text itself does not draw it, and their reading is best offered as an application: the nameless kinsman as a picture of the law. The law has a prior and legitimate claim upon us, for we are lawbreakers and its demand is just. But it cannot set us free without giving up its own just demands. The law can condemn; it cannot save.

So when the law steps back, another Redeemer steps forward, willing to bear the full cost in himself, to be 'impaired,' indeed to be made poor that we might be made rich. The nearer redeemer's 'I cannot' makes way for Boaz's 'I will,' and points beyond Boaz to the One who said, 'I lay down my life for the sheep.'

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sandal ceremony seals the transfer of the right of redemption. Boaz declares before the elders and all the people that he has acquired the land and Ruth as his wife, to perpetuate the name of the dead. The people pronounce a rich blessing, invoking Rachel, Leah, Tamar and Perez.
verseByVerse.theology: Boaz steps forward as the willing redeemer who bears the full cost gladly. The sandal ceremony (Deut 25:9) and the public declaration make the redemption legally complete and witnessed. The blessing sets this redemption within God's covenant purposes leading to David and the Messiah.
verseByVerse.examples: Boaz models the willing redeemer who counts the beloved worth every cost. The community's blessing reminds us that redemption and marriage are matters of covenant community, witnessed and celebrated by the people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this was the custom in former times in Israel concerning redeeming and exchanging: to confirm a transaction, the one drew off his sandal and gave it to the other, and this was the manner of attesting in Israel. So when the redeemer said to Boaz, "Buy it for yourself," he drew off his sandal. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator explains an ancient custom for a later generation, a sign that the book was written some time after the events. To confirm a transaction of redemption or exchange, one man drew off his sandal and gave it to the other: a legally binding, publicly witnessed gesture of transfer, a kind of ancient signature.

The custom echoes Deuteronomy 25:9, where the widow removed the sandal of a kinsman who refused levirate marriage, as a sign of his shame; here the gesture is voluntary and dignified, simply a formal transfer of the right of redemption.

With this simple act the nearer kinsman relinquishes his claim, and the path is clear for Boaz. Ruth's redemption is no shadowy arrangement but a fully witnessed, formally sealed transfer. The transaction that will lead to David, and to David's greater Son, is sealed with the humble removal of a shoe in a village gate.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Boaz said to the elders and all the people, "You are witnesses this day that I have bought from the hand of Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech and all that belonged to Chilion and to Mahlon. Also Ruth the Moabite, the widow of Mahlon, I have bought to be my wife, to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance, that the name of the dead may not be cut off from among his brothers and from the gate of his native place. You are witnesses this day." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz's public declaration rings with the joy of a redeemer who counts the cost worth paying. "You are witnesses this day" frames the whole community as legal witnesses. The crown of his declaration is Ruth: where the nearer kinsman recoiled at the cost, Boaz embraces it.

His stated purpose is "that the name of the dead may not be cut off." He acts not for his own gain but to preserve a dead kinsman's line, fill the emptiness of Naomi's house, and give Ruth a home. For the final time she is "Ruth the Moabite," the outsider made wife, bound to the line that will produce the Messiah.

The gospel pattern shines here: the willing redeemer pays the full price to make the destitute his own and give his name to one who had none. Christ has bought his bride at infinite cost, given her his name, and brought life where there was only the cutting off of death. And we, as we read, are witnesses to a redemption that pictures our own.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the people who were at the gate and the elders said, "We are witnesses. May the LORD make the woman, who is coming into your house, like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. May you act worthily in Ephrathah and be renowned in Bethlehem, and may your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, because of the offspring that the LORD will give you by this young woman." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The community responds with a threefold blessing that ties this marriage into the whole story of God’s saving work.

First, that Ruth be "like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel." To liken Ruth the Moabite to the matriarchs is a stunning affirmation of her full inclusion; the foreigner is welcomed as a mother of the nation. Second, worthiness and renown for Boaz in Ephrathah and Bethlehem.

Third, and most remarkably, "the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah." Tamar, like Ruth, was a widow in an irregular situation, who through unusual means (Gen 38) secured offspring for the line of Judah and bore Perez, from whom Boaz descended. God has often advanced his purposes through unlikely women and irregular circumstances. The mention of Perez points forward to the genealogy that closes the book: "the offspring that the LORD will give you" will be Obed, then Jesse, then David, then, in the fullness of time, the Messiah.

Three women from outside Israel, Tamar (probably a Canaanite), Rahab and Ruth, stand in the line of Christ (Matt 1:3–5), monuments to the grace of a God who delights to redeem the outsider and to write his glory through the unlikely.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — The Redeemer's Son and the Line of David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Boaz marries Ruth, and the LORD gives her conception; she bears a son. The women bless Naomi, calling the child a restorer of life and praising Ruth as worth more than seven sons. Naomi takes the child to her bosom, and the women name him Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David.
verseByVerse.theology: The reader hears in v. 13 the familiar note of Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah: life as God's gift, not a human achievement. And the closing genealogy reveals the hidden providence of the whole book as God's plan to bring forth the messianic king.
verseByVerse.examples: Naomi, who returned empty and bitter, now holds a grandchild to her bosom, the proof that God's providence was for her all along. The women's praise of Ruth as 'more to you than seven sons' honors the foreign daughter-in-law above what that culture counted the highest blessing. No act of loyal love is wasted with God. And for readers whose arms are still empty: the LORD who gave Ruth a son does not give every longed-for child, and childlessness is never a mark of his disfavour. Naomi’s deepest gift was not finally a baby but a Redeemer, and that gift is offered to every believer, with a place in Christ’s own family that no loss can take away (Mark 3:35).

verseByVerse.quote: So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. And he went in to her, and the LORD gave her conception, and she bore a son. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a single verse the redemption is completed: the worthy man and the worthy woman are joined, and the threshing-floor pledge is fulfilled.

The most significant phrase follows: "the LORD gave her conception." The narrator could simply have said Ruth conceived; instead he ascribes it emphatically to the LORD. Ruth had been married to Mahlon for some years in Moab (the family stayed about ten) without bearing a child (1:4–5). Scripture never calls her barren, but her childless years had seemed an insurmountable obstacle.

This is the crowning truth of the book. The God who seemed hidden throughout, who worked behind the 'coincidences' and never spoke directly in the narrative, is named as the giver of life, the author of the redemption that has unfolded. Every human act in the story, Ruth's loyalty and Boaz's redemption, has been the instrument; but the life itself, the future itself, is the gift of God. The empty womb is filled by the hand of heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer, and may his name be renowned in Israel! He shall be to you a restorer of life and a nourisher of your old age, for your daughter-in-law who loves you, who is more to you than seven sons, has given birth to him." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women of Bethlehem, who asked in shock "Is this Naomi?", now gather to bless her, completing the great reversal of the book.

The God whom Naomi accused of dealing bitterly with her is praised as the One who has not left her without a redeemer. The "redeemer" here is most immediately the child himself, who as heir will perpetuate the line and secure Naomi's future, though the words also take in what Boaz has done. The woman who had no husband, no sons and no future now has a grandchild who will sustain her and fill her empty years.

Then a remarkable tribute: Ruth, who loves her, "is more to you than seven sons." In a culture that prized sons above all, and with seven the number of completeness, this was the highest possible honor. The Moabite outsider, labeled by her foreignness at every turn, is celebrated as the supreme blessing of Naomi's life. The bitter woman is blessed, and the God she accused has redeemed her beyond all her hopes. Hesed has triumphed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Naomi took the child and laid him on her lap and became his nurse. And the women of the neighborhood gave him a name, saying, "A son has been born to Naomi." They named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The image is almost unbearably tender. The woman who cried "call me Mara" and "the LORD has brought me back empty" now holds a child to her bosom. The empty arms are full at last.

"A son has been born to Naomi": through Ruth's child the line of Elimelech, which seemed utterly extinguished in the deaths of chapter 1, is restored and continued. The bitterness of chapter 1 is answered by the blessing of chapter 4; the emptiness is filled to overflowing.

Then the genealogical climax: Obed "was the father of Jesse, the father of David." David, the greatest king of Israel, the man after God's own heart, the king to whom God promised an everlasting throne (2 Sam 7), traces his ancestry through this very child, through Boaz the redeemer and Ruth the Moabite. God was never merely arranging the comfort of two widows; he was forging a link in the chain that leads to the throne of David and beyond, to the manger.
verseByVerse.note: Jesse's family stayed in Bethlehem, where Samuel would find David (1 Sam 16:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — The Genealogy: From Perez to David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book closes with a ten-generation genealogy from Perez (son of Judah) to David, revealing the story of Ruth and Boaz as a vital link in the line leading to Israel's great king and, ultimately, to the Messiah.
verseByVerse.theology: The genealogy unlocks the book's purpose. The story of Ruth is not merely a beautiful tale of loyalty and redemption; it is part of the messianic line. The list from Perez to David sets the redemption of a Moabite widow within God’s promise that the ruler would come from Judah (Gen 49:10). The hidden providence of the whole book is revealed as God's purpose to bring forth the Son of David, the King of kings.
verseByVerse.examples: God works across generations, weaving individual lives of faith into purposes that span centuries. Ruth and Boaz could not see that their loyal love would lead to David and to Christ; they simply acted faithfully in their moment. So we may be faithful in our own small stories, trusting that God is weaving them into a design we cannot yet see. The smallest acts of hesed echo into eternity.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the generations of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron, Hezron fathered Ram, Ram fathered Amminadab, Amminadab fathered Nahshon, Nahshon fathered Salmon, Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed, Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book closes not with Naomi and the child but with a ten-name genealogy from Perez to David, and this is no dry appendix but the theological crown of the work.

Perez is the son of Judah by Tamar, whom the people named in their blessing (4:12), another outsider through whom God advanced the messianic line. Ten generations, a complete number, culminate in the final name: David.

Everything has been building toward this. The famine, the bereavements, the vow on the road from Moab, the 'chance' arrival in Boaz's field, the bold request at the threshing floor, the willing redeemer at the gate, the child given by the LORD: all of it was God's hidden work to bring forth David, the recipient of the promise of an everlasting throne (2 Sam 7:12–16).

The New Testament carries the line one decisive step further: Matthew 1:5 places Ruth the Moabite explicitly in the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the Son of David. The tiny story of a destitute foreign widow and a worthy redeemer leads from the barley fields of Bethlehem to the manger of Bethlehem, from the gleaning of grain to the bread of life. The God of hidden providence, who seemed absent and silent through the suffering, was all along weaving redemption, not only for Naomi and Ruth, but for the world. Grace all the way down, and grace all the way home.

Ten names cover several centuries, so the list probably skips generations, as biblical genealogies often do. Matthew names Rahab as Boaz’s mother (Matt 1:5): an outsider’s son married an outsider, and both are in the line of Christ.

4.theology:
The Willing Redeemer and the Law That Cannot Save. The nearer redeemer has the right and resources but lacks the willingness: 'I cannot redeem it, lest I impair my own inheritance' (v. 6). Many have seen in him a picture of the law, which has a just claim on us but cannot redeem (Rom 8:3); the text does not say so, and the application is fair only if held lightly. Boaz steps forward as the willing redeemer who gladly bears the full cost. So Christ, the eternal Son with every right and infinite resources, was supremely willing to be 'impaired' (to become poor, to bear our sin, to bear the law's curse) that we might be redeemed.

The God Who Fills the Empty. The God who seemed hidden is named in v. 13 as the giver of life, and the woman who returned 'empty' holds a child to her bosom (v. 16). This is Romans 8:28 told as a story: God working all things, even the deaths and the emptiness, for the good of those who love him and are called according to his purpose.

Grace to the Outsider in the Line of the Messiah. Ruth the Moabite, labeled by her foreignness to the very end, stands in the genealogy that leads to David and, through Matthew 1:5, to Jesus Christ. Alongside Tamar and Rahab, she foreshadows the gospel that will reach every nation.
4.examples:
Then: The transaction at the gate reflects ancient Israel's legal customs: the elders as witnesses, land redemption (Lev 25:25) intertwined with levirate marriage (Deut 25:5–10), and the sandal that sealed the transfer. Redemption and marriage were matters for the whole community of God’s people, not merely private arrangements.

Now: Boaz confronts us with the question every redeemer faces: is the beloved worth the cost? We can answer as he did only because we have first been answered: Christ counted us worth his own life, and his Spirit now makes self-giving love possible where calculation once ruled. And the closing genealogy teaches us to live faithfully in our own small stories, trusting that God weaves them into purposes that span generations. Naomi could not see, in her bitterness, that her empty arms would one day cradle the ancestor of the Messiah. So we trust the God of hidden providence, who fills the empty, redeems the outsider, and brings forth from our ordinary faithfulness a glory we cannot yet imagine.
